overview:
The term "Śrāvakācāra" (often written Shravakachara) designates a distinctive Jain textual genre that codifies the ideal conduct, vows, and daily discipline of the lay follower (śrāvaka/śrāvikā). Etymologically, it combines śrāvaka—“one who listens,” used for the Jain householder who receives teachings from monks—with ācāra, “conduct” or “practice.” Together, Śrāvakācāra refers to the normative pattern of lay life as envisioned by Jain ascetic authors, especially within the Digambara tradition, though cognate materials exist in Śvetāmbara sources as well.

Historically, the Śrāvakācāra corpus emerges as a parallel to monastic codes, articulating śrāvakadharma (lay dharma) alongside munidharma (monastic dharma). It translates the central Jain soteriological framework—right faith (samyagdarśana), right knowledge (samyagjñāna), and right conduct (samyakcāritra), the ratnatraya or “three jewels”—into a graded path suitable for householders who remain engaged in family, work, and social obligations. Texts in this genre specify the fundamental ethical restraints (such as non‑violence, truthfulness, non‑stealing, chastity, and non‑attachment), the minor vows (guṇavrata), and the disciplinary or training vows (śikṣāvrata), as well as ritual observances, fasting practices, and the progressive stages (pratimā) of lay advancement.

Within the Digambara tradition, the Śrāvakācāra corpus is especially prominent and includes seminal works such as Ācārya Samantabhadra’s Ratnakaraṇḍaka‑śrāvakācāra, Āśādhara’s Sāgāradharmāmṛta, and other medieval manuals that systematize lay religious law. These texts do more than list moral precepts: they function as a theology of ordinary life, regulating everyday decisions—diet, business, speech, ritual participation—through the lens of karma theory and the pursuit of liberation. Modern scholarship has emphasized that Śrāvakācāra operates analogously to Dharmaśāstra in Hindu traditions, providing a normative legal‑ethical framework for householders while remaining grounded in Jain metaphysics and ascetic ideals.

Although the label "Śrāvakācāra" is most closely associated with Digambara literature, the underlying concern with lay conduct is pan‑Jain. Śvetāmbara canonical texts such as the Upāsakadaśāh (the seventh Aṅga) present narrative and doctrinal models of ideal lay behavior that fulfill the function of a Śrāvakācāra without being explicitly categorized as such. These works depict exemplary householders who embody right faith and rigorous ethical discipline while remaining in the world, thereby integrating laity into the broader Jain spiritual economy.

The Śrāvakācāra corpus is structurally rich. Typically, a text begins by defining right faith and distinguishing genuine teachers, scriptures, and deities from false paths. It then expounds right knowledge through classification of scriptural domains (such as the four anuyogas: narrative, cosmological, ethical, and metaphysical expositions). Finally, it details right conduct in terms of graded vows, ritual practices, and the eleven pratimās, which mark increasing renunciation and discipline for laypersons. Some texts also discuss the ideal of sallekhanā—voluntary, passionless death under specific conditions—as the culmination of austerity for both monks and householders, though its interpretation and practical application are subject to careful ethical and legal scrutiny in contemporary discourse.

In the broader history of Jainism, the Śrāvakācāra genre has played a crucial role in shaping lay identity, community norms, and the interface between ascetic authority and household life. It offers a bridge between the radical non‑violence and renunciation of monastic ideals and the pragmatic realities of commerce, family, and social responsibility. As such, the Śrāvakācāra corpus remains central to understanding how Jain communities have negotiated the tension between world‑renunciation and world‑engagement across centuries.

primary_sources.title: Ratnakaraṇḍaka‑śrāvakācāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Samantabhadra (Digambara)
primary_sources.notes: Comprising approximately 150 verses, this is widely regarded as one of the earliest and most influential Digambara Śrāvakācāra texts. It systematically presents the path of dharma for lay followers, emphasizing acquisition and safeguarding of the three jewels—right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct—as the means to liberation from worldly suffering. The work defines right faith as correct belief in the true teacher (āpta/deva), scripture (āgama/śāstra), and preceptor (guru), and provides criteria to distinguish authentic from counterfeit authorities. It then elaborates right knowledge through engagement with Jain scriptural categories and right conduct through abstention from the five major sins (injury, falsehood, stealing, unchastity, attachment to possessions), observance of three guṇavratas and four śikṣāvratas, and progression through eleven pratimās (stages of lay conduct). The text also treats sallekhanā—voluntary, passionless death under specific conditions—as the final fruit of austerity, though contemporary application of this ideal requires guidance from qualified teachers and attention to modern ethical and legal frameworks.

primary_sources.title: Sāgāradharmāmṛta (selected chapters)
primary_sources.author: Āśādhara (13th century Digambara)
primary_sources.notes: Āśādhara’s Sāgāradharmāmṛta is a major medieval Digambara treatise within the Śrāvakācāra tradition. Scholarly studies highlight especially the sixth chapter, which describes the ideal daily routine of a Jain householder, illustrating how dharma permeates ordinary life. The text codifies lay conduct as a form of religious law, governing actions such as eating, business dealings, ritual observance, and interaction with ascetics. It builds on the definition of dharma found in earlier Śrāvakācāra works—understood as the force that elevates beings from transmigration to liberation—and integrates the triad of right faith, knowledge, and conduct into a detailed schedule of practices. Modern academic analysis compares Sāgāradharmāmṛta to Dharmaśāstra, arguing that it provides a ‘theology of ordinary life’ for Jain householders, while remaining firmly rooted in Jain doctrines of karma, non‑violence, and renunciation.

primary_sources.title: Upāsakadaśāh (Seventh Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon)
primary_sources.author: Attributed within the canonical redaction; traditional authorship not specified
primary_sources.notes: Although not labeled as a Śrāvakācāra text in traditional classification, the Upāsakadaśāh functions as a canonical Śvetāmbara counterpart to the lay conduct genre. As the seventh Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon, it presents doctrinal expositions and narrative exempla that construct an ideal image of the lay follower (upāsaka/śrāvaka). The text situates laity within the theological and philosophical framework of the monastic compilers, showing how householders can embody right faith and rigorous ethical discipline while remaining in worldly life. Contemporary scholarship has argued that Upāsakadaśāh represents one of the earliest consolidated attempts to articulate a discourse on lay conduct within the core canon, thereby providing an important comparative lens for understanding the later Digambara Śrāvakācāra corpus.

misconceptions.myth: The Śrāvakācāra corpus is only a simple list of moral maxims for lay Jains.
misconceptions.reality: In fact, Śrāvakācāra texts constitute a sophisticated legal‑ethical and theological framework for household life. They integrate metaphysics, karma theory, scriptural hermeneutics, and graded vows into a comprehensive vision of how laypersons pursue liberation while remaining in the world. Modern scholarship describes this tradition as a form of religious law and a ‘theology of ordinary life,’ not merely a collection of moral aphorisms.

misconceptions.myth: Śrāvakācāra literature belongs exclusively to the Digambara tradition and has no relevance for Śvetāmbara Jains.
misconceptions.reality: While the term "Śrāvakācāra" and many key texts are indeed Digambara, the concern with codifying lay conduct is shared across Jain traditions. Śvetāmbara canonical works such as the Upāsakadaśāh perform a similar function by depicting and regulating ideal lay behavior, even if they are not formally categorized under the Śrāvakācāra label. Comparative study shows substantial overlap in ethical content and soteriological aims.

misconceptions.myth: Śrāvakācāra texts encourage extreme ascetic practices for all laypeople, regardless of health, age, or circumstances.
misconceptions.reality: Śrāvakācāra works present graded vows and stages of renunciation, recognizing that householders have varied capacities and responsibilities. Ideals such as prolonged fasting or sallekhanā are framed within specific doctrinal and situational criteria and traditionally require guidance from qualified teachers. Contemporary Jain communities and scholars emphasize that medical, mental‑health, legal, and family considerations must be carefully weighed, and that no text should be used to justify coercive or harmful practices.
